title: Dinacharya — The Ayurvedic Daily Regimen
content: Dinacharya refers to the sacred daily routine prescribed by Ayurveda to align circadian physiology with natural solar and planetary rhythms. Traditional daily practices include: 1. Brahma Muhurta: Waking approximately 48 to 96 minutes before sunrise, when atmospheric Vata and Sattvic clarity predominate. 2. Saucha: Evacuation of natural bowel and bladder urges. 3. Danta Dhavana & Jihwa Nirlekhana: Cleaning teeth with herbal powders (Neem, Babool) and gently scraping the tongue from back to front with copper or stainless steel scraper to remove overnight toxic film (Ama). 4. Gandusha / Kavala: Oil pulling with warm sesame or coconut oil for 5 to 15 minutes to strengthen teeth, gums, and oral microbiota. 5. Netra Prakshalana & Nasya: Washing eyes with cool water or triphala wash, followed by 1-2 drops of warm sesame oil or Anu Taila in each nostril to lubricate nasal pathways. 6. Abhyanga: Warm oil self-massage before bathing to soothe Vata, nourish skin, and enhance circulation. 7. Vyayama: Moderate physical exercise (up to half of one's capacity, indicated by mild perspiration on forehead and nose). 8. Snana: Cleansing warm bath.

title: Ritucharya — Seasonal Regimen and Biological Adjustments
content: Ritucharya is the systematic adjustment of diet, clothing, and activity according to the six seasons (Ritus) recognized in traditional Indian climatology: 1. Shishira (Late Winter): strong Agni; hearty, nourishing, unctuous foods are suitable. 2. Vasanta (Spring): environmental warming liquefies accumulated Kapha; light, easily digestible foods, barley, honey, and dry massage (Udvartana) are recommended to prevent congestion. 3. Grishma (Summer): scorching sun depletes bodily moisture and spikes Pitta; cooling, sweet, liquid foods, hydration, and avoiding intense midday sun are advised. 4. Varsha (Monsoon): dampened digestive fire requires light, warm, sour-salty foods and boiled water to prevent Vata accumulation and microbial distress. 5. Sharad (Autumn): sudden solar heat triggers Pitta vitiation; bitter (Tikta), sweet (Madhura), and astringent (Kashaya) herbs and foods with ghee are traditionally taken. 6. Hemanta (Early Winter): robust digestion permits rich, warming, sweet foods. Adapting to seasonal transitions prevents cyclical sickness.

title: Ahara — Ayurvedic Dietary Principles and the Six Tastes (Shad Rasa)
content: Ayurveda regards Ahara (food) as the foremost pillar of longevity ('Mahabheshaja' or the greatest medicine). Food is classified according to six fundamental tastes (Shad Rasa): 1. Madhura (Sweet): nourishing, builds tissues, pacifies Vata and Pitta, increases Kapha. 2. Amla (Sour): stimulates appetite and digestion, pacifies Vata, increases Pitta and Kapha. 3. Lavana (Salty): retains moisture, aids digestion, pacifies Vata, increases Pitta and Kapha. 4. Katu (Pungent/Spicy): clears sinuses and stimulates circulation, pacifies Kapha, increases Vata and Pitta. 5. Tikta (Bitter): detoxifying, purifying, cooling, pacifies Pitta and Kapha, increases Vata. 6. Kashaya (Astringent): drying, heals tissues, pacifies Pitta and Kapha, increases Vata. A balanced meal should ideally include all six tastes in suitable proportion, eaten in a calm environment only after the previous meal has been fully digested.
source: Ministry of AYUSH — Dietary Guidelines for Swastha Vritta

title: Viruddha Ahara — Incompatible Food Combinations
content: Viruddha Ahara refers to food items that, when combined, processed, or consumed under improper conditions, possess mutually conflicting biological properties that disrupt digestion and induce chronic Ama formation. Classical examples of incompatible combinations include: 1. Milk combined with sour fruits, citrus, or melons (which curdles milk proteins and deranges gut fermentation); 2. Equal quantities by weight of honey and ghee (traditionally considered toxic due to conflicting thermal and chemical reactions); 3. Heating honey above 40°C / boiling honey (which creates sticky, unassimilable biochemical molecules according to Charaka); 4. Milk consumed with fish (conflicting thermal potencies: fish is hot/Ushna, milk is cold/Sheeta); 5. Eating cold, iced water immediately before, during, or after warm meals (which extinguishes Jatharagni).

title: Nidra — Sleep as the Second Pillar of Life
content: In Ayurveda, Trayopastambha refers to the three supportive pillars of life: Ahara (nutrition), Nidra (sleep), and Brahmacharya (regulated vitality and sensory moderation). Charaka declares: 'Happiness, nourishment, strength, virility, knowledge, and life itself depend upon proper sleep.' Sound sleep (Sukha Nidra) allows cellular restoration, deep tissue rejuvenation, and psychological integration of memories. Daytime sleep (Divaswapna) is generally contraindicated in adults as it sharply vitiates Kapha and Pitta and causes channel obstruction, except during severe summer heat or for convalescents and the elderly. Sleeping on the left side (Vamkukshi) after light digestion is traditionally recommended to optimize digestive fire (located on the left) and promote efficient breathing through the right nostril (Surya Nadi).

title: Yoga, Pranayama, and Meditation in Ayurvedic Health
content: Ayurveda and Yoga are sister sciences rooted in Vedic philosophy. While Yoga addresses spiritual emancipation and mental mastery through the eight limbs (Ashtanga Yoga), Ayurveda provides the physical and physiological basis for this practice. In traditional wellness, specific Asanas (postures) and Pranayama (breath regulation) balance doshas: 1. Nadi Shodhana (Alternate Nostril Breathing) balances both hemispheres, calms aggravated Vata, and centers the nervous system; 2. Sheetali and Sheetkari (Cooling Breath) pacify excess internal Pitta and cool body temperature; 3. Bhastrika and Kapalabhati stimulate sluggish Agni, expel excess mucus, and pacify heavy Kapha. Meditation (Dhyana) reduces mental Rajas (restlessness) and Tamas (inertia), fostering Sattva (pure cognitive clarity and inner peace).

title: Rajaswala Paricharya — Ayurvedic Menstrual Cycle Care & Female Wellness
content: In Ayurveda, menstruation is revered as a sacred monthly cleansing and physiological reset governed primarily by Apana Vayu (the sub-dosha of Vata controlling downward movement in the pelvic region) and Artava Dhatu. The classical lifestyle and dietary regimen prescribed for balanced, pain-free period cycles is termed Rajaswala Paricharya (detailed in Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita Sharirasthana). Foundational guidelines for women's menstrual cycle health include: 1. Rest and Gentle Pace: Physical rest during the initial 2-3 days calms Apana Vata; heavy strenuous exercise, long journeys, and intense stress push Apana Vata upward (Pratiloma), triggering menstrual cramps (Kashtartava), pelvic spasms, and irregular cycles. 2. Warm, Light, Nourishing Diet: Eat freshly cooked, warm, easily digestible meals (such as warm moong dal khichdi, cooked rice with a touch of ghee, and warm vegetable soups). Strictly avoid cold drinks, ice, raw salads, excess chili, and deep-fried foods that vitiate Vata and Pitta. 3. Carminative Spices for Cramp Relief: Herbal teas prepared with cumin (Jeera), fennel (Saunf), dry ginger (Shunthi), and ajwain (carom seeds) naturally relax uterine muscles, reduce bloating, and ease menstrual pain. 4. Warmth and Comfort: Using a warm heating pad or gently applying warm sesame oil to the lower abdomen and lower back soothes pelvic spasms. 5. Classical Female Herbs: Revered Ayurvedic herbs such as Shatavari (Asparagus racemosus) for hormonal balance and Apana Vata nourishment, Ashoka (Saraca asoca) for uterine tone and cycle regularity, and classical tonics like Ashokarishta are traditionally utilized under qualified Ayurvedic supervision.
